opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, I was working on computer vision, and around 2012 to 2015 we all watched deep learning start to change the field. AlexNet had come out, and suddenly the results from neural networks were far better than the hand-crafted methods many of us had spent years on. It was clear to me that this was where the field was heading, and I wanted to be fully in it.

To do deep learning seriously you need two things: compute, and people who think about the problem from the ground up. NVIDIA had both. GPUs were really the engine of the deep learning revolution. Researchers everywhere were training their models on NVIDIA hardware. So being at the company that builds that engine felt like being at the center of the action. You can see where the compute is going, and you have access to resources that are hard to find elsewhere.

The other part was the research culture. NVIDIA Research was growing, and the leadership was very open to letting researchers explore ambitious, long-term ideas, not just things tied to a product next quarter. For me that was very attractive. I was especially interested in generative models. GANs had just appeared, and I felt that teaching machines to create images, and eventually whole worlds, was a deep and exciting problem. NVIDIA is fundamentally a graphics company, so generative modeling and graphics fit together naturally. There was a real intersection between what I wanted to study and what the company cared about.

So it wasn't only about having more GPUs, although that certainly helped. It was the sense that the company's mission and the direction of AI research were converging, and I wanted to be part of that convergence. Looking back, it was one of the best decisions I've made.

fable-5.1.text:
When I was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, I was doing computer vision work, and this was right around 2012 to 2015, when deep learning was starting to change everything. I remember training my first networks and realizing that what was limiting me wasn't ideas, it was compute. I had maybe one or two GPUs, and every experiment felt like waiting in line.

And I started thinking about who was actually sitting at the center of this shift. Everybody in the community, whether they were at Google, Facebook, or a university, was running on NVIDIA GPUs. So NVIDIA had a very unusual position. It wasn't competing with any one lab; it was underneath all of them. If deep learning was going to become as big as I believed it would, the company making the hardware would have both the resources and a very strong reason to invest heavily in the research itself.

The other thing was that NVIDIA at that time was just beginning to build a serious research group. Bill Dally had come over from Stanford to lead it, and it felt like joining something early rather than slotting into a mature organization. That appealed to me. At a place like MERL, which I really respected, the mission was tied to the parent company's products, which were things like factory automation and elevators. Important, but not where I wanted my research to land.

So the combination was very attractive: essentially unlimited access to the hardware I needed, a leadership that understood why fundamental research mattered, and a feeling that the work could reach the whole field rather than one product line. I also, frankly, liked that it was a bit of a bet. In 2016, NVIDIA was still known as a gaming company to most people. But I thought if I was right about where things were going, it would be the best place to be, and if I was wrong, I'd still have learned a lot about building systems at scale. I was fortunate that it turned out to be the former.

NVIDIA felt like a natural place to pursue it because computing is such an important part of the work. You need to be able to run experiments, test ideas, and learn from the results. Being at a company where that computing platform was central to the business was very appealing. I also saw an opportunity to work with strong researchers and connect our research to technology that other people could use.
